reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A less common cause of mesenteric ischaemia, most often involving the superior mesenteric vein and its tributaries
Presentation is frequently subacute with vague, poorly localised abdominal pain evolving over days, in contrast to the abrupt onset of arterial occlusion
The classic teaching is pain out of proportion to abdominal findings, at least early before infarction and peritonitis develop
A hypercoagulable state, whether inherited thrombophilia, malignancy, or acquired prothrombotic conditions, underlies many cases and should be sought
Local factors such as portal hypertension, intra-abdominal inflammation or infection, recent surgery, and pancreatitis also predispose
Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice, showing thrombus in the mesenteric or portal veins, bowel wall oedema, and signs of compromised perfusion
Prompt systemic anticoagulation is the mainstay when there is no infarction, and it improves outcomes and limits propagation
Bowel infarction, peritonitis, or clinical deterioration mandates surgical exploration with resection of non-viable bowel
reference.pathophysiology: Mesenteric venous thrombosis occurs when thrombus obstructs venous outflow from the bowel, most commonly in the superior mesenteric vein. Impaired venous drainage raises intestinal capillary and interstitial pressure, producing bowel wall oedema, arterial inflow compromise, and progressive congestion. If flow is not restored, transmural ischaemia and infarction ensue, with translocation of bacteria, peritonitis, and sepsis. It is usually driven by hypercoagulable states (primary thrombophilia, malignancy) or local factors such as portal hypertension, abdominal sepsis or inflammation, and recent surgery. The extent of collateral drainage and the speed of thrombus propagation determine whether ischaemia remains reversible.
additionalDifferentials: Acute arterial mesenteric ischaemia (embolic or thrombotic)
Other causes of acute abdomen (e.g. appendicitis, diverticulitis)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen with venous phase to identify venous thrombus and bowel compromise
Duplex ultrasound of the portal and mesenteric veins in selected cases
Laboratory markers of ischaemia including lactate and acid-base status
Thrombophilia screen and evaluation for underlying malignancy
Assessment for portal hypertension and intra-abdominal inflammatory sources
redFlags: Peritonism, rising lactate, or haemodynamic instability indicating bowel infarction and the need for emergency surgery
Pain out of proportion to examination raising early suspicion before overt signs appear
Gastrointestinal bleeding or clinical deterioration during treatment
Extension into the portal vein or evidence of extensive bowel involvement
reference.prognosis: When diagnosed before infarction and treated promptly with anticoagulation, mesenteric venous thrombosis has a better prognosis than acute arterial mesenteric ischaemia. Delayed diagnosis with established bowel necrosis carries high morbidity and mortality, and recurrence risk depends on the underlying prothrombotic cause and duration of anticoagulation.
pitfalls: Attributing subacute nonspecific abdominal pain to benign causes and delaying imaging
Failing to obtain venous-phase CT and missing the venous thrombus
Delaying anticoagulation in the absence of infarction
Not investigating for an underlying thrombophilia or malignancy after the acute event
